exercise.name: Band Alternating Front Raise

reference.title: Band Alternating Front Raise
reference.listing: Video (movement reference only; the page could not be fetched from the authoring environment (the proxy refused gymvisual.com), so the movement follows the name and standard coaching)

exercise.laterality: Alternating (right then left in one loop)

breathing.pattern: Breathe out as each arm rises, breathe in as it lowers.
breathing.cadence: About 2 s up, short pause, about 2 s down, each arm in turn

prescription.load: Band tension is user-chosen; light; the band is hardest at shoulder height
prescription.progression: Add reps, then a stronger band or the feet wider on the band; slower lowering

cues.text: Stand on the middle of the band, feet hip width; hold an end in each hand in front of the thighs, palms facing the thighs, elbows soft.
Breathe out and raise one arm straight forward, palm down; the other hand stays at the thigh.
Stop at shoulder height, arm about parallel to the floor; no leaning back or twisting.
Lower slowly in about 2 s against the band, then switch arms.
Brief pause with both hands at the thighs, then repeat.

mistakes.mistake: Leaning back or twisting the trunk to lift the arm
mistakes.fix: Brace the trunk, keep the hips and shoulders square; use a lighter band.
Stop at about 90 degrees (the range tested by Coratella 2020).
Keep the shoulders down and the neck long.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the band snap the arm down

kinematics.norm: Palms down (pronated) is the common gym form; Coratella 2020 tested a neutral humerus
Upright and still; no lean back (clinical opinion)

Elastic tension rises as the band stretches, so the load is highest where the band is longest; at matched effort, elastic tubing and dumbbells gave similar muscle activity in upper-body exercises (Andersen 2010); with the band under the feet the load is highest at shoulder height
2 s up, 0.5 s pause, 2 s down (Coratella 2020)

sources.title: GymVisual #25614, Band Alternating Front Raise, video (movement reference)
Coratella et al. 2020, an electromyographic analysis of lateral raise variations and frontal raise in competitive bodybuilders (Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(17):6015)
Campos et al. 2020, different shoulder exercises affect the activation of deltoid portions in resistance-trained individuals (J Hum Kinet 75:5-14)

Andersen, Andersen, Mortensen, Poulsen, Bjornlund and Zebis 2010, muscle activation and perceived loading during rehabilitation exercises: comparison of dumbbells and elastic resistance (Phys Ther 90(4):538-549)

cautions: Stop if sharp pain, a pinching feeling in the front or top of the shoulder, numbness or tingling occurs.
Band tension is user-chosen: pick one you can control for every rep with good form.

Check the band for nicks or tears before each set and make sure it cannot slip off its anchor (under the feet, round the upright). Stand firmly on its middle so it cannot slip out from under the feet.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Shoulder pain: raise with palms facing each other (neutral grip) and stop below shoulder height.
Low-back strain: do it seated or with the back against a wall.
progressions: Stronger band, or dumbbell front raise.

muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: Prime mover (shoulder flexion), one arm at a time. The frontal raise gave the highest anterior deltoid activity in the lifting phase among the raises tested (Coratella 2020, dumbbells); at matched effort elastic tubing gave shoulder activity similar to dumbbells (Andersen 2010).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_l: Prime mover (shoulder flexion), one arm at a time. The frontal raise gave the highest anterior deltoid activity in the lifting phase among the raises tested (Coratella 2020, dumbbells); at matched effort elastic tubing gave shoulder activity similar to dumbbells (Andersen 2010).
muscleNotes.pec_r: The clavicular (upper) head flexes the shoulder; it was most active in the frontal raise and low in all lateral raises (Coratella 2020).
muscleNotes.pec_l: The clavicular (upper) head flexes the shoulder; it was most active in the frontal raise and low in all lateral raises (Coratella 2020).
muscleNotes.lat_deltoid_r: Helps hold the arm up; medial deltoid activity was among the lowest in the frontal raise (Coratella 2020).
muscleNotes.lat_deltoid_l: Helps hold the arm up; medial deltoid activity was among the lowest in the frontal raise (Coratella 2020).
muscleNotes.serratus_r: Rotates the shoulder blade up as the arm rises.
muscleNotes.serratus_l: Rotates the shoulder blade up as the arm rises.
muscleNotes.upper_traps_r: Supports the shoulder blade; activity was low in the frontal raise (Coratella 2020).
muscleNotes.upper_traps_l: Supports the shoulder blade; activity was low in the frontal raise (Coratella 2020).
muscleNotes.core: Keeps the trunk from rocking back or twisting as one arm rises.
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_r: Hold the trunk upright against the forward load.
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_l: Hold the trunk upright against the forward load.
muscleNotes.forearm_extensors_r: Hold the wrists level with the palms down.
muscleNotes.forearm_extensors_l: Hold the wrists level with the palms down.
